key_insight: The paper argues that the main bottleneck in autonomous scientific discovery is no longer the agent workflow itself, but the design of the agent environment. By engineering the right resources, constraints, and interfaces, LLM agents can more effectively explore, validate, and improve scientific solutions.
problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of making LLM-based agents reliably useful for autonomous scientific discovery, especially when current progress is limited more by environment setup than by hand-crafted action sequences or fixed workflows.
method: Frame scientific discovery as an optimization problem where agents iteratively propose, test, and refine solutions.
Shift focus from manually prescribing agent steps to designing the execution environment, including resources, constraints, and interaction interfaces.
Use environment engineering to create conditions that better support self-improving agent behavior and scalable discovery.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this reframes how to build effective scientific agents: success may depend more on environment design than on increasingly complex prompting or workflow orchestration. This can simplify agent development while improving reliability, adaptability, and discovery performance.
visual_elements: A comparison diagram showing 'workflow engineering' vs 'environment engineering' as the main bottleneck shift.
A pipeline graphic of agent-driven discovery: propose -> validate -> iterate -> improve.
An environment box model highlighting resources, constraints, tools, and interfaces.
A before/after chart showing improved discovery outcomes with better environment design.
paper_title: EurekAgent: Agent Environment Engineering is All You Need For Autonomous Scientific Discovery
paper_authors: Amy Xin, Jiening Siow, Junjie Wang, Zijun Yao, Fanjin Zhang
